## Trust boundary

- Discover and pin authorization-server issuer identity before persisting or redeeming credentials.
- Validate a returned iss value and never reuse credentials across issuers.
- Send an appropriate application_type and prefer Client ID Metadata Documents over deprecated dynamic registration.
- Make consent scopes align with pm read, mutation, workspace, extension, task, and resource authority.
- Validate transport headers and custom x-mcp-header mappings against injection, confused deputy, SSRF, replay, downgrade, and proxy-cache threats.
- Propagate traceparent, tracestate, and baggage only through allowlisted metadata with privacy limits and redaction.
- Keep stdio local trust behavior distinct from remote HTTP authorization rather than silently treating one as the other.
MCP remote authorization and observability: issuer-bound credentials, client metadata documents, consent, header security, and OpenTelemetry propagation

Define and implement the 2026-07-28 remote MCP trust boundary for Streamable HTTP, including authorization discovery, issuer validation, registration migration, consent, trace context, and abuse resistance.

Authorization-server discovery and issuer pinning prevent credentials from being reused or redeemed at a different issuer; Present iss values are validated and dynamic registration fallback is bounded behind Client ID Metadata Document preference; application_type, redirect URI, scopes, consent, refresh, revocation, and re-registration behavior have positive and negative tests; Header mappings, proxies, caches, traces, logs, errors, and telemetry cannot leak tokens, secrets, workspace paths, or private resource content; traceparent, tracestate, and baggage propagation follows explicit allowlists, byte limits, and redaction; A threat model and real Streamable HTTP integration suite gate release
Make every remote request attributable, authorized, consented, privacy-bounded, and traceable without credential or context leakage
Organizations can expose pm remotely without unsafe token reuse, redirect ambiguity, header injection, or opaque failures
The revision tightens issuer and application-type validation, binds credentials to authorization servers, prefers Client ID Metadata Documents, and defines trace-context propagation
